h: Tennyson Country, Roman Walls and a Woodland Cinema
p: Horncastle has deep roots. The town grew up on the site of a Roman fort, and fragments of the old Roman walls still survive in the town centre, with a section on show in the library. It's a quiet thrill to stumble on a slice of the ancient world in a little Lincolnshire market town. Horncastle was also known for centuries for its great horse fair, a famous event that drew dealers from all over the country.

For the wildlife park, a slow, relaxed approach suits it best. Give children time at each enclosure to really watch, rather than racing on to the next. Pack a picnic, wellies if it's been wet, and a coat, because wind across the Wolds can be sharp. Small, independent parks rely on their visitors, so buying a drink or a treat on site is a simple way of supporting them.

The Wolds are Tennyson country. Alfred, Lord Tennyson, one of the most famous poets of the Victorian age, was born in 1809 at Somersby, a tiny village a few miles east of Horncastle, where his father was rector. Driving the quiet lanes past the church gives you a feel for the landscape that shaped his early poems.

Just south-west of town, Woodhall Spa has a wonderful treat for film fans: the Kinema in the Woods, a charming old cinema set among pine trees that still shows films today, sometimes with an organ interlude. It's a lovely, old-fashioned way to finish a day out.
